claim: Standard phylogenetic models do not allow mutations to feedback and shape trees.
source: While standard phylogenetic models do not allow mutations to feedback and shape trees, birth-death models can account for this feedback by letting the fitness of lineages depend on their type.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a contrast to the proposed approach.

claim: Birth-death models can account for feedback between mutations and tree structure by letting the fitness of lineages depend on their type.
source: While standard phylogenetic models do not allow mutations to feedback and shape trees, birth-death models can account for this feedback by letting the fitness of lineages depend on their type.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the basis for the proposed approach.

claim: Multi-type birth-death models have only been applied to cases where a lineage's fitness is determined by a single character state.
source: To date, these multi-type birth-death models have only been applied to cases where a lineage's fitness is determined by a single character state.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of previous work.

claim: The MFBD model can accurately estimate the fitness of lineages from phylogenies.
source: Although approximate, we show that we can accurately estimate the fitness of lineages and site-specific mutational fitness effects from phylogenies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The MFBD model can accurately estimate site-specific mutational fitness effects from phylogenies.
source: Although approximate, we show that we can accurately estimate the fitness of lineages and site-specific mutational fitness effects from phylogenies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Many mutations are neutral.
source: Studies exploring the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) in a wide range of organisms have revealed that, while many mutations are neutral, a smaller but significant fraction have substantial effects on fitness (Sanjuán et al., 2004; Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007; Visher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A smaller but significant fraction of mutations have substantial effects on fitness.
source: Studies exploring the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) in a wide range of organisms have revealed that, while many mutations are neutral, a smaller but significant fraction have substantial effects on fitness (Sanjuán et al., 2004; Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007; Visher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Standard phylogenetic models assume that the mutation process driving sequence evolution is independent of the other evolutionary processes giving rise to the tree.
source: While all of these models assume sequences evolve along an underlying phylogenetic tree representing their shared common ancestry, all also assume that the mutation process driving sequence evolution is independent of the other evolutionary processes giving rise to the tree.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of existing models.

claim: The independence assumption implies that mutations do not feedback and affect the fitness of lineages in the tree.
source: This independence assumption implies that mutations do not feedback and affect the fitness of lineages in the tree, such that lineages carrying highly beneficial mutations are just as likely to survive and produce sampled descendants as lineages riddled with deleterious mutations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the independence assumption.

claim: Under the independence assumption, lineages carrying highly beneficial mutations are just as likely to survive and produce sampled descendants as lineages riddled with deleterious mutations.
source: This independence assumption implies that mutations do not feedback and affect the fitness of lineages in the tree, such that lineages carrying highly beneficial mutations are just as likely to survive and produce sampled descendants as lineages riddled with deleterious mutations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the independence assumption.

claim: The independence assumption allows for tractable statistical models.
source: While questionable in terms of biological realism, independence between the tree generating process and the mutation process allows for tractable statistical models.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for the independence assumption.

claim: The assumption of independence between the mutation and tree generating processes may be unproblematic if mutations are truly neutral or do not contribute to substantial fitness differences among lineages.
source: The assumption of independence between the mutation and tree generating processes may be unproblematic in certain scenarios, such as if mutations are truly neutral or do not contribute to substantial fitness differences among lineages.
evidence: This is stated as a condition under which the independence assumption is reasonable.

claim: Macroevolutionary tree generating processes like speciation and extinction play out on longer timescales than the substitution process fixing or removing mutations within a population.
source: A common argument invoked in defense of ignoring non-neutral mutations is that macroevolutionary tree generating processes like speciation and extinction play out on longer timescales than the substitution process fixing or removing mutations within a population (Bustamante, 2005).
evidence: This is cited as a common argument from the literature.

claim: Separation-of-timescales arguments do not hold when segregating mutations contribute to substantial fitness variation between lineages in a phylogeny.
source: But such separation-of-timescales arguments do not hold when segregating mutations contribute to substantial fitness variation between lineages in a phylogeny, such as for rapidly evolving microbes where several different mutant strains can co-circulate.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the separation-of-timescales argument.

claim: For rapidly evolving microbes, the tree generating and mutation processes occur on the same timescale.
source: In these cases, the tree generating and mutation processes occur on the same timescale, and the fitness effects of mutations can feedback and shape the branching structure of a phylogeny (Kaplan et al., 1988; Nicolaisen and Desai, 2012; Neher and Hallatschek, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The fitness effects of mutations can feedback and shape the branching structure of a phylogeny in rapidly evolving microbes.
source: In these cases, the tree generating and mutation processes occur on the same timescale, and the fitness effects of mutations can feedback and shape the branching structure of a phylogeny (Kaplan et al., 1988; Nicolaisen and Desai, 2012; Neher and Hallatschek, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ignoring non-neutral evolution may introduce biases into phylogenetic inference when mutations contribute to substantial fitness variation.
source: Ignoring non-neutral evolution in this case may introduce biases into phylogenetic inference.
evidence: This is stated as a potential problem with ignoring non-neutral evolution.

claim: Fitness differences among lineages can be correlated with ancestral genotypes.
source: But perhaps more importantly, fitness differences among lineages can be correlated with ancestral genotypes, providing information about the molecular basis of adaptive evolution we would otherwise ignore.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the proposed approach.

claim: Under the MTBD model, mutations can directly impact the fitness of a lineage in the phylogeny by altering its birth or death rate.
source: Under this approach, mutations can directly impact the fitness of a lineage in the phylogeny by altering its birth or death rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the MTBD model.

claim: For a single evolving site or other character state, the joint likelihood of the phylogeny together with the observed tip states can be computed exactly under the MTBD model.
source: For a single evolving site or other character state, the joint likelihood of the phylogeny together with the observed tip states can be computed exactly under the MTBD model (Maddison et al., 2007; Stadler and Bonhoeffer, 2013; Kühnert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MTBD approach is impractical for more than a few non-neutrally evolving sites due to the need to track all possible genotypes as separate types in the state space of the model.
source: However, this approach is impractical for more than a few non-neutrally evolving sites due to the need to track all possible genotypes as separate types in the state space of the model.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the MTBD model.

claim: The MFBD model considers how mutations at multiple sites contribute to a lineage's overall fitness without the need to track all possible genotypes in sequence space.
source: We therefore explore an approximate birth-death model that considers how mutations at multiple sites contribute to a lineage's overall fitness, without the need to track all possible genotypes in sequence space.
evidence: This is stated as the key innovation of the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model allows inference of the fitness effects of individual mutations from the branching structure of a phylogeny.
source: This approach allows us to infer the fitness effects of individual mutations and the fitness of any particular lineage at any time (based on its inferred ancestral genotype) from the branching structure of a phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model allows inference of the fitness of any particular lineage at any time based on its inferred ancestral genotype.
source: This approach allows us to infer the fitness effects of individual mutations and the fitness of any particular lineage at any time (based on its inferred ancestral genotype) from the branching structure of a phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model tracks molecular evolution at each site and computes the probability that each site occupies each state.
source: In the approach described below and outlined in Figure 1D, we therefore track molecular evolution at each site, computing the probability that each site occupies each state, and then approximate the probability of a lineage being in any particular genotype based on these site probabilities.
evidence: This is stated as the approach used by the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model approximates the probability of a lineage being in any particular genotype based on marginal site probabilities.
source: In the approach described below and outlined in Figure 1D, we therefore track molecular evolution at each site, computing the probability that each site occupies each state, and then approximate the probability of a lineage being in any particular genotype based on these site probabilities.
evidence: This is stated as the approach used by the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model computes the expected fitness of a lineage by marginalizing over the fitness of each genotype weighted by its approximate probability.
source: To compute the expected fitness of a lineage, we can then sum, or marginalize, over the fitness of each genotype weighted by its approximate probability.
evidence: This is stated as the approach used by the MFBD model.

claim: The MFBD model assumes that all sites evolve independently of one another when approximating genotype probabilities.
source: This approximation assumes that all sites evolve independently of one another, which is not generally true because mutations at different sites are linked together in genotypes with shared ancestral histories, creating correlations among sites that we ignore.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the MFBD model.

claim: Mutations at different sites are linked together in genotypes with shared ancestral histories, creating correlations among sites.
source: This approximation assumes that all sites evolve independently of one another, which is not generally true because mutations at different sites are linked together in genotypes with shared ancestral histories, creating correlations among sites that we ignore.
evidence: This is stated as a biological fact that the MFBD model ignores.

claim: At very high mutation rates, correlations between sites quickly break down so that sites evolve effectively independently of one another.
source: Conversely, at very high mutation rates, correlations between sites quickly break down so that sites evolve effectively independently of one another, such that the error introduced by the MFBD also decreases as the mutation rate becomes very high.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the behavior of the MFBD model at high mutation rates.

claim: The error introduced by the MFBD model decreases as the mutation rate becomes very high.
source: Conversely, at very high mutation rates, correlations between sites quickly break down so that sites evolve effectively independently of one another, such that the error introduced by the MFBD also decreases as the mutation rate becomes very high.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the four genotype model analysis.

claim: Tracking how lineages transition between fitness classes in fitness space does not improve the approximation of E_n relative to simply ignoring changes in fitness along unobserved lineages.
source: Interestingly, tracking how lineages transition between fitness classes in fitness space does not improve the approximation relative to simply ignoring changes in fitness along unobserved lineages (Figure 4A–C; dashed lines).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 4A-C.

claim: The accuracy and precision of estimated fitness effects varies considerably across sites.
source: The accuracy and precision of the estimated fitness effects varies considerably across sites, as shown for a representative phylogeny with five evolving sites in Figure 5.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 5.

claim: The estimated posterior median fitness effects are well correlated with their true values.
source: Overall, the estimated posterior median fitness effects are well correlated with their true values, although the strength of this correlation decreases as the number of sites increases (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6A-C.

claim: The strength of correlation between estimated and true fitness effects decreases as the number of sites increases.
source: Overall, the estimated posterior median fitness effects are well correlated with their true values, although the strength of this correlation decreases as the number of sites increases (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6A-C.

claim: Coverage of the 95% credible intervals on fitness effects increased from 71.0% to 72.8% to 77.4% as the number of sites increased from 2 to 5 to 10.
source: Coverage of the 95% credible intervals on the other hand increased from 71.0 to 72.8% to 77.4%.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the simulations.

claim: Fitness effects are underestimated for sites at which the mutant allele is at low frequency among sampled individuals.
source: While there is no systematic directional bias, fitness effects are underestimated for sites at which the mutant allele is at low frequency among sampled individuals and overestimated for sites where the mutant allele is at high frequencies.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the simulations.

claim: Fitness effects are overestimated for sites where the mutant allele is at high frequencies.
source: While there is no systematic directional bias, fitness effects are underestimated for sites at which the mutant allele is at low frequency among sampled individuals and overestimated for sites where the mutant allele is at high frequencies.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the simulations.

claim: The same phenomena of under- and overestimation of fitness effects at low and high frequencies is observed under the exact MTBD model.
source: This however appears to be an intrinsic feature of estimating fitness effects from the branching structure of a phylogeny, as the same phenomena is observed under the exact MTBD model with two sites and four genotypes (Figure 6D), and the estimates made under the approximate MFBD model are highly correlated with estimates made under the exact MTBD model (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6D-E.

claim: The estimates made under the approximate MFBD model are highly correlated with estimates made under the exact MTBD model.
source: This however appears to be an intrinsic feature of estimating fitness effects from the branching structure of a phylogeny, as the same phenomena is observed under the exact MTBD model with two sites and four genotypes (Figure 6D), and the estimates made under the approximate MFBD model are highly correlated with estimates made under the exact MTBD model (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: Accuracy of fitness effect estimates decreased when the mutant allele at a given site was at low or high frequencies.
source: Across all sites and simulations, accuracy decreased when the mutant allele at a given site was at low or high frequencies, and there was considerably more uncertainty for sites where the mutant allele was at very low frequencies (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6F.

claim: There was considerably more uncertainty for sites where the mutant allele was at very low frequencies.
source: Across all sites and simulations, accuracy decreased when the mutant allele at a given site was at low or high frequencies, and there was considerably more uncertainty for sites where the mutant allele was at very low frequencies (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 6F.

claim: The Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) binds to cells during viral cell entry.
source: The Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) binds to cells during viral cell entry and is therefore thought to be a key determinant of viral fitness in different hosts.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about Ebola virus.

claim: The Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) is thought to be a key determinant of viral fitness in different hosts.
source: The Ebola virus glycoprotein (GP) binds to cells during viral cell entry and is therefore thought to be a key determinant of viral fitness in different hosts.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about Ebola virus.

claim: Urbanowicz et al. (2016) analyzed a large set of naturally occurring amino acid mutations in the GP isolated from patients during the 2013–16 epidemic in Western Africa.
source: Previously, (Urbanowicz et al., 2016) analyzed a large set of naturally occurring amino acid mutations in the GP isolated from patients during the 2013–16 epidemic in Western Africa.
evidence: This is cited as previous work.

claim: Several mutant genotypes dramatically increased viral infectivity relative to the Makona genotype isolated during the earliest stages of the epidemic.
source: Several mutant genotypes dramatically increased viral infectivity relative to the Makona genotype isolated during the earliest stages of the epidemic.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Urbanowicz et al. (2016) found evidence for epistatic interactions between several GP mutations.
source: Because Urbanowicz et al. (2016) found evidence for epistatic interactions between several of these mutations, we estimated the fitness of these eight genotypes rather than site-specific mutational fitness effects.
evidence: This is cited as a finding from previous work.

claim: The A82V mutation occurred shortly after the epidemic started in 2013 and gave rise to lineage B.
source: Shortly after the epidemic started in 2013, the A82V mutation occurred and gave rise to lineage B, which then spread to Sierra Leone, Liberia and Mali.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Lineage B spread to Sierra Leone, Liberia and Mali.
source: Shortly after the epidemic started in 2013, the A82V mutation occurred and gave rise to lineage B, which then spread to Sierra Leone, Liberia and Mali.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Urbanowicz et al. (2016) found that the A82V mutation increases infectivity by 2–3 fold in cell culture.
source: (Urbanowicz et al., 2016) found that the A82V mutation increases infectivity by 2–3 fold in cell culture.
evidence: This is cited as a finding from previous work.

claim: At the population-level, the A82V mutation increases transmissibility by only 5% relative to the Makona genotype.
source: At the population-level, this mutation appears to have a less dramatic effect, increasing transmissibility by only 5% relative to the Makona genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: The P330S mutation appears to have temporarily decreased the fitness of the main surviving clade in lineage A.
source: The P330S mutation appears to have temporarily decreased the fitness of the main surviving clade in lineage A, although mutations N107D and G480D later rescue the fitness of this lineage, consistent with the findings of Urbanowicz et al. (2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Mutations N107D and G480D rescue the fitness of the lineage carrying P330S.
source: The P330S mutation appears to have temporarily decreased the fitness of the main surviving clade in lineage A, although mutations N107D and G480D later rescue the fitness of this lineage, consistent with the findings of Urbanowicz et al. (2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The R410S mutation did not have an immediate effect on fitness.
source: Meanwhile, the R410S mutation occurred within lineage B but did not have an immediate effect on fitness.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: R410S appears to epistatically interact with mutation K439E.
source: However, R410S appears to epistatically interact with mutation K439E, which occurs twice along the same lineage carrying the R410S mutation and in this genetic background increases infectivity 2–3 fold in cell culture.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: K439E occurs twice along the same lineage carrying the R410S mutation and in this genetic background increases infectivity 2–3 fold in cell culture.
source: However, R410S appears to epistatically interact with mutation K439E, which occurs twice along the same lineage carrying the R410S mutation and in this genetic background increases infectivity 2–3 fold in cell culture.
evidence: This is stated as a finding combining the phylogenetic analysis with previous experimental work.

claim: The A82V+R410S+K439E genotype had the highest population-level fitness.
source: We estimate that the A82V+R410S+K439E genotype had the highest population-level fitness, but only increased fitness by 14% relative to the Makona genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: The A82V+R410S+K439E genotype only increased fitness by 14% relative to the Makona genotype.
source: We estimate that the A82V+R410S+K439E genotype had the highest population-level fitness, but only increased fitness by 14% relative to the Makona genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Three mutations (R29K, T230A and I371V) occurred in the A82V genetic background but were not estimated to have further increased the fitness of the A82V genotype.
source: Three other mutations, R29K, T230A and I371V, also occurred in the A82V genetic background, but were not estimated to have further increased the fitness of the A82V genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: There is no evidence that transmission rates differed by location in the Ebola epidemic.
source: We found no evidence that transmission rates differed by location; relative transmission rates were 1.01 (95% CI: 0.97–1.05) in Sierra Leone and 0.99 (95% CI: 0.94–1.04) in Liberia compared with Guinea.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis with geographic effects.

claim: All mutant genotypes had higher estimated fitness relative to the Makona genotype under the model with geographic effects.
source: All mutant genotypes had higher estimated fitness relative to the Makona genotype under the model with geographic effects due to a lower estimated fitness of the Makona genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis with geographic effects.

claim: The rank order of genotypic fitness values is consistent across models with and without geographic effects.
source: However, the rank order of genotypic fitness values is consistent across models (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: The population level fitness of all eight Ebola genotypes agree with their fitness in cell culture in terms of the sign or direction of their effects.
source: Overall, the population level fitness of all eight genotypes agree with their fitness in cell culture in terms of the sign or direction of their effects, but these genotypes had much greater fitness relative to the Makona genotype in cell culture than at the population level.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Ebola genotypes had much greater fitness relative to the Makona genotype in cell culture than at the population level.
source: Overall, the population level fitness of all eight genotypes agree with their fitness in cell culture in terms of the sign or direction of their effects, but these genotypes had much greater fitness relative to the Makona genotype in cell culture than at the population level.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Ebola analysis.

claim: Lee et al. (2018) estimated the relative preference for each amino acid residue at all sites in the HA protein in cell culture using deep mutational scanning (DMS).
source: Lee et al. (2018) recently estimated the relative preference for each amino acid residue at all sites in the HA protein in cell culture using a reverse genetics approach known as deep mutational scanning (DMS).
evidence: This is cited as previous work.

claim: The fitness effect of mutating one amino acid to another is expected to correlate strongly with the relative preference for each amino acid in DMS experiments.
source: The fitness effect of mutating one amino acid to another is expected to correlate strongly with the relative preference for each amino acid in these experiments.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on the nature of DMS experiments.

claim: There is no apparent relationship between the estimated population-level fitness effects of the 17 most abundant H3N2 mutations and their in vitro effects.
source: We found no apparent relationship between the estimated population-level fitness effects of these mutations and their in vitro effects, although there is agreement that most of these mutations are nearly neutral (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis and supported by Figure 8A.

claim: Most of the 17 most abundant H3N2 mutations are nearly neutral.
source: We found no apparent relationship between the estimated population-level fitness effects of these mutations and their in vitro effects, although there is agreement that most of these mutations are nearly neutral (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis and supported by Figure 8A.

claim: The MCMC algorithm never converged on a stable posterior distribution for several H3N2 mutations due to strong correlations between mutations in their estimated fitness effects.
source: Although the 95% credible intervals on our estimates are narrow, these results need to be interpreted with extreme caution because our MCMC algorithm never converged on a stable posterior distribution for several mutations (Effective Sample Size < 10) due to strong correlations between mutations in their estimated fitness effects.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the H3N2 analysis.

claim: Many H3N2 mutations occur only once in the phylogeny and share the same ancestry and genetic background as other mutations.
source: This is likely due to the fact that many of these mutations occur only once in the phylogeny and share the same ancestry and therefore genetic background as other mutations in the phylogeny (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the convergence problems and supported by Figure 8B.

claim: The fitness effects predicted by DMS correlate strongly with the maximum frequency that naturally occurring mutations reach in the human population.
source: While our population-level estimates did not correlate with the in vitro data, the fitness effects predicted by DMS correlate strongly with the maximum frequency that naturally occurring mutations reach in the human population (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited as a finding from previous work.

claim: Population-level fitness grows slowly and roughly linearly with mutations to more preferred amino acids.
source: Population-level fitness grows slowly and roughly linearly with mutations to more preferred amino acids (Figure 9; inset).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 9 inset.

claim: When mutational fitness effects are aggregated across all sites, there are substantial fitness differences between H3N2 lineages.
source: Nevertheless, when mutational fitness effects are aggregated across all sites, there are substantial fitness differences between lineages (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by Figure 9.

claim: Relative to a hypothetical lineage bearing the consensus sequence, H3N2 fitness ranges from 0.84 to 1.04 across lineages.
source: Relative to a hypothetical lineage bearing the consensus sequence, fitness ranges from 0.84 to 1.04 across lineages with many lineages having a relative fitness less than one, indicating a slightly deleterious mutation load.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: Many H3N2 lineages have a relative fitness less than one, indicating a slightly deleterious mutation load.
source: Relative to a hypothetical lineage bearing the consensus sequence, fitness ranges from 0.84 to 1.04 across lineages with many lineages having a relative fitness less than one, indicating a slightly deleterious mutation load.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: The MFBD model informed by DMS data fits the H3N2 phylogeny substantially better than a model assuming all mutations are neutral.
source: Accounting for these fitness differences results in the MFBD model informed by the DMS data fitting the H3N2 phylogeny substantially better (Log likelihood: −4184) than a model assuming all mutations are neutral (Log likelihood: −7510).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: H3N2 lineages predicted to be more fit tend to persist between influenza seasons.
source: As would be expected, lineages predicted to be more fit also tend to persist between influenza seasons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: A lineage with higher than average fitness circulates in 2009 and 2010 during the H1N1 pandemic.
source: Most notably, a lineage with higher than average fitness circulates in 2009 and 2010 during the H1N1 pandemic.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: The lineage circulating during the H1N1 pandemic carries the T228A mutation, which is predicted to have a large beneficial effect in the DMS experiments.
source: This lineages carries the T228A mutation, which is predicted to have a large beneficial effect in the DMS experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the H3N2 analysis with DMS-informed fitness.

claim: The T228A mutation may have conferred an advantage that helped seasonal H3N2 compete with the pandemic H1N1 virus.
source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that this mutation may have conferred an advantage that helped seasonal H3N2 compete with the pandemic H1N1 virus.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings.

claim: The MFBD model approximation generally works well and only produces significant errors in extreme situations.
source: While our approach is not exact in that it approximates genotype probabilities by assuming sites evolve independently when computing the marginal fitness of a lineage, we have shown that this approximation generally works well and only produces significant errors in rather extreme situations, such as the four genotype model with very strong selection or epistasis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation analyses.

claim: The fitness effects of specific mutations can be estimated from simulated phylogenies under the MFBD with accuracy comparable to an exact multi-type birth death model.
source: Using our approach, we demonstrated that the fitness effects of specific mutations can be estimated from simulated phylogenies under the MFBD with accuracy comparable to an exact multi-type birth death model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation analyses.

claim: The MFBD model provides a new, statistically powerful way of incorporating adaptive molecular evolution into phylodynamics.
source: The MFBD model therefore provides a new, statistically powerful way of incorporating adaptive molecular evolution into phylodynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the contribution of the work.

claim: The MFBD model allows exploitation of phylogenetic information about adaptive evolution that most methods for inferring selection from patterns in sequence data ignore.
source: The MFBD model allows us to exploit phylogenetic information about adaptive evolution that most methods for inferring selection from patterns in sequence data ignore.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the MFBD model.

claim: Codon-substitution models and mutation-selection models are the most widely used approach for inferring selection.
source: Currently, codon-substation models (Goldman and Yang, 1994; Muse and Gaut, 1994) and the related class of mutation-selection models (Yang and Nielsen, 2008) are by far the most widely used approach for inferring selection.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: Codon-substitution models rely on comparing sequence substitution patterns such as the dN/dS ratio.
source: These approaches rely on comparing sequence substitution patterns such as the dN/dS ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitutions across sites.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of codon-substitution models.

claim: On shorter timescales relevant to evolution within a population, substitution patterns like the dN/dS ratio are relatively insensitive to selection pressures.
source: But on the shorter timescales relevant to evolution within a population, substitution patterns like the dN/dS ratio are relatively insensitive to selection pressures and may produce misleading inferences of selection (Kryazhimskiy and Plotkin, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of codon-substitution models with a citation.

claim: Comparing the evolutionary dynamics of lineages with and without a mutation allows inference of whether that mutation confers a competitive advantage.
source: In contrast, comparing the evolutionary dynamics of lineages with and without the mutation allows us to infer if that mutation confers a competitive advantage.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the phylodynamic approach.

claim: Considering the branching pattern of phylogenies provides additional information about molecular evolution not visible from substitution patterns in sequence data alone.
source: Thus, considering the branching pattern of phylogenies provides additional information about molecular evolution not visible from substitution patterns in sequence data alone.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the phylodynamic approach.

claim: How fitness measured in the lab translates to fitness in nature is largely unknown.
source: While new technologies increasingly allow researchers to quantify mutational fitness effects in vitro or even in vivo (Zanini and Neher, 2013; Thyagarajan and Bloom, 2014), how fitness measured in the lab translates to fitness in nature is largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The epidemic potential of emerging pathogens often depends on new adaptive mutations.
source: This is especially pertinent for emerging pathogens whose epidemic potential often depends on new adaptive mutations (Antia et al., 2003; Longdon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Phylodynamic approaches like the MFBD model that can quantify fitness at the host population level are greatly needed.
source: Phylodynamic approaches like the MFBD model that can quantify fitness at the host population level are therefore greatly needed, as they offer a means to assess the epidemiological significance of mutant lineages.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the work.

claim: Fitness measured in the lab will generally agree with fitness in nature in terms of the sign of the effect.
source: Extrapolating from our experience with Ebola, where the population-level fitness effects of each mutant genotype we considered matched the sign of their effect in cell culture, we suspect that fitness measured in the lab will generally agree with fitness in nature.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the Ebola analysis.

claim: Mutations that increase replication or cellular infectivity within hosts should generally promote transmissibility between hosts.
source: This seems reasonable, as mutations that increase replication or cellular infectivity within hosts should generally promote transmissibility between hosts (e.g. Quinn et al., 2000; Fraser et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a reasonable expectation with citations.

claim: There is no reason to believe that transmission rates will increase linearly or even monotonically with increasing within-host growth rates.
source: But at the same time, there is no reason to believe that transmission rates will increase linearly or even monotonically with increasing within-host growth rates.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat to the expectation above.

claim: The magnitude of fitness effects might often greatly differ across scales (in vitro vs. population level).
source: We therefore expect that the magnitude of fitness effects might often greatly differ across scales, as we found for the A82V glycoprotein mutation in Ebola.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on the Ebola findings.

claim: Diehl et al. (2016) found that A82V only slightly increases viral titers in Ebola patients.
source: Interestingly, (Diehl et al., 2016) found that A82V only slightly increases viral titers in Ebola patients, which is likely a much better proxy for transmissibility than cellular infectivity, lending support to our more moderate estimates at the population level.
evidence: This is cited as supporting evidence from previous work.

claim: Viral titers in patients are likely a much better proxy for transmissibility than cellular infectivity.
source: Interestingly, (Diehl et al., 2016) found that A82V only slightly increases viral titers in Ebola patients, which is likely a much better proxy for transmissibility than cellular infectivity, lending support to our more moderate estimates at the population level.
evidence: This is stated as an inference to support the population-level estimates.

claim: The inference problems for H3N2 likely stem from the fact that many mutations occur only once in the phylogeny and in the same genetic background as other mutations.
source: We believe that these inference problems likely stem from the fact that many of these mutations occur only once in the phylogeny and in the same genetic background as other mutations in the HA protein.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the inference problems.

claim: The shared phylogenetic ancestry of mutations creates an identifiability problem akin to the problem of collinearity in regression-type models.
source: The shared phylogenetic ancestry of mutations creates an identifiability problem akin to the problem of collinearity in more standard regression-type models.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the inference problems.

claim: Background variation in fitness arising from deleterious mutations plays a large role in determining which H3N2 lineages ultimately persist.
source: Most lineages were reconstructed to have a slightly deleterious mutation load, consistent with earlier reports that background variation in fitness arising from deleterious mutations, not just antigenic mutations, plays a large role in determining which H3N2 lineages ultimately persist (Illingworth and Mustonen, 2012; Luksza and Lässig, 2014; Koelle and Rasmussen, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with previous work cited.

claim: There are likely mutations in other genomic segments besides HA with large fitness effects in H3N2.
source: Moreover, the fitness variation uncovered by our analysis likely represents only the 'tip of the iceberg', since there are likely mutations in other genomic segments besides HA with large fitness effects (Raghwani et al., 2017), which we did not consider.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the analysis with a citation.

claim: Increasing the number of sites under consideration increases the complexity of the genetic background in which mutations occur.
source: Increasing the number of sites under consideration also increases the complexity of the genetic background in which mutations occur due to the increased probability of mutations being linked to other mutations rather than occurring in isolation.
evidence: This is stated as a general challenge for inference.

claim: Increasing the number of sites leads to strong correlations between the fitness effects of different sites in an increasingly high dimensional parameter space.
source: This leads to strong correlations between the fitness effects of different sites in an increasingly high dimensional parameter space, making statistical inference challenging, especially using MCMC methods.
evidence: This is stated as a general challenge for inference.

claim: Spurious correlations may arise due to additional, unmodeled sources of fitness variation.
source: Spurious correlations may also arise due to additional, unmodeled sources of fitness variation.
evidence: This is stated as a potential problem with the current approach.

claim: The MFBD should be extended to account for unmodeled sources of fitness variation.
source: In the future, the MFBD should therefore be extended to account for unmodeled sources of fitness variation.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.

claim: The fitness effects of individual mutations need to be interpreted carefully unless they occur in multiple genetic backgrounds and confounding sources of fitness variation can be accounted for.
source: Until such a principled approach is implemented, the fitness effects of individual mutations need to be interpreted carefully unless they occur in multiple genetic backgrounds and confounding sources of fitness variation can be accounted for, as we tried to do for Ebola by including potentially confounding geographic fitness effects.
evidence: This is stated as a caution for interpreting results.

claim: The MFBD model offers a powerful means to explore many questions not previously possible with strictly neutral phylodynamic models.
source: In spite of these shortcomings, we believe the MFBD model offers a powerful means to explore many questions not previously possible with strictly neutral phylodynamic models.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the contribution of the work.

claim: It may be possible to infer the distribution of fitness effects across sites using the MFBD model.
source: Even if the fitness effects of individual mutations are not identifiable, it may still be possible to infer the distribution of fitness effects across sites, a key determinant of adaptive evolution that has only been explored in a few systems (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a potential application with a citation.

claim: The MFBD model can be used to compare the fitness of a mutation or lineage across different environments.
source: The MFBD model can also be used to compare the fitness of a mutation or lineage across different environments, such as in different hosts of a pathogen.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application.

claim: The MFBD is not limited to exploring sequence evolution and is generalizable to any discrete character state.
source: Finally, the MFBD is not limited to exploring sequence evolution, as the model is generalizable to any discrete character state, including phenotypic, geographic or environmental characters.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of the model.

claim: The MFBD model can be thought of as a multi-trait, multi-type birth-death model.
source: Thus, more generally, our model can be thought of as a multi-trait, multi-type birth-death model that can be used to explore how different molecular and non-molecular characters interact to shape the overall fitness of lineages in a phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as a general characterization of the model.
